How I Stopped Getting FOMO From Social Media
By
Nina Davuluri
November 30, 2022
Getty Images
In this op-ed, Nina Davuluri explores FOMO, and how social media influences our internal validation.
Have you ever woken up to a massive flow of TikTok videos, Instagram posts, and stories highlighting a party you weren’t invited to? I have, and it hurts.
A year ago, I experienced this and felt an overwhelming amount of
FOMO
— which stands for fear of missing out, or, exclusion. I sat crying on my bed as my
thoughts
swirled out of control: “Why wasn’t I invited? Do people not like me? What did I do wrong? Am I not valuable? Am I not enough?” It took a long time for me to come to the conclusion that none of this shameful line of questioning was true. Looking back at that person from a year ago, I so badly want to tell her that her value will not come from being on a guest list.
In June 2022, I gave a TED Talk titled
The Cost of Beauty From A Miss America
, and having so much FOMO last year was an inspiring moment for that speech. It might seem ridiculous to be triggered by something as trivial as a party, but this party was
Diwali
. Not being invited to one particular Diwali celebration made me feel like I was no longer “relevant,” and because of that feeling, I decided to log off social media as best I could.
How to Use Social Media Without Feeling Like Sh*t
An excerpt from Sammy Nickalls' book "Log Off: Self-Help for the Extremely Online."
With my newfound free time (which, not surprisingly, was
a lot
once I cut out social media), I deeply reflected on my internal and external drivers of happiness. In doing so, I realized that I was grappling with the ways in which social media reinforced a competitive spirit within myself. If I felt this way, I
had an inclination
that others must be feeling this way too.
Social media explicitly reminds us of exclusivity and shows a highlight reel of all the rooms you’re
not
in. You’re either “in the room” or watching from the digital sidelines, and that feeling of watching from the sidelines is often more painful than not being invited in the first place.
In an
emotional sense
, you may feel you aren’t ‘good enough’ to be in the room. But if we pause and ask ourselves, “Why does this invitation matter so much to me? And what is it that I need to prove to the world by posting this picture on social media?” What will often emerge from that reflection are influences that oppress our sense of belonging and self-worth. By participating in the world of social media, we assign
outsized value
to proof-of-attendance and perpetuate the concept of exclusivity. This perpetuation of exclusivity repels inclusivity.
As I reflected on my day-after, tear-filled Instagram scrolling session, I realized I was giving
too much power
to the perceived status and social media validation of having been invited. I was weighing this recognition more than the joy and fulfillment of work done outside of the limelight.
Of course, I’ve also fed into this when I was invited to an event — posting photos just to show I was there. It hurts me knowing that there may be others who were also looking for external validation, and may have been feeling worse having seen my social media content. If we allow external factors (like invites, followers, and compliments) to determine our self-worth, we are wasting energy on the wrong things.
I kept coming back to the question: Having experienced feelings of exclusion, which we’ve
all
experienced to some degree, is this feeling something we want to knowingly perpetuate? Further, internal vs. external validation is a well
researched
concept. So why are the concepts so hard to separate?
To find an answer for myself, I had to
step away from social media
altogether. What I’ve discovered over this past year without social media is that I was focusing on the external validation and ignoring my internal validation. The likes, reposts, tags, and shares — they made me feel good in the moment. They made me feel good enough that I wanted to post again, but they left me empty by the next day. What was even worse, was that I wasn’t just hurting myself, but I was perpetuating this emptiness for everyone who
wasn’t
in the room. Others were unintentionally doing the same to me, and down the rabbit hole we all went. This hurts others, it hurts me, and it might be hurting you.
Stepping away helped me become more mindful. The likes matter less, and the more I force myself to think harder about what I share, the more fulfilled I actually feel. Even better, that fulfillment came because I was simply sharing some of the work I was doing — emphasis on the work, not the clout.
The main argument for social media is the power of connection. But, as an even bigger bonus, I’ve been able to form deeper and more valuable connections than ever before. I was forced (and trying) to engage more directly, and more thoughtfully. Less time was spent curating my highlight reel and feeling jealous of everyone else’s. Instead, I was so much more locked in on meeting people virtually and in person, and wanting to organically hear what they were up to instead of watching a curated snapshot.
I’ve slowly reintegrated my social media diet, but this time being more deliberate. I’m not invulnerable — I still get FOMO, and it still stings for a moment. But I’m in a place where I can remind myself: the things I’m not included in are not a measure of my worth. We are worth more than an invitation! But that rabbit hole I mentioned? We’re all susceptible to it, and in order to climb out, we have to recognize that we collectively have the power to influence our personal algorithm of our value and mental health.
Let us slide into your DMs.
